## Introduction 

This section will close out our brief tour of deeper learning models by discussing image detection and compression, two important applications which pull us deeper into the realm of neural networks^[At least it doesn't force us to go deeper into our own neural networks. Scary.].

## The MNIST Dataset

For our applications, we'll be using the Modified National Standards and Technology (MNIST) dataset which contains greyscale intensities for 60,000 different 28x28 pixel images of handwritten digits 0-9. You can load this by downloading the `mnist_train.rds` file from github and loading it into R using the `readRDS` function^[The dataset is large enough where storing and loading it as a csv takes too much time. An RDS file is more compact.].

```{r}
df_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/mnist_train.rds"

mnist_df = readRDS(url(df_url))
```

Each row contains the [0,1] greyscale values for the image written as a $28 \times 28 = 784$ list of numbers as well as the actual digit classification (0,1,2,etc.) for the image. You can view one of them by "unravelling" the image values as follows:

```{r}
img1 = matrix(
  as.numeric(mnist_df[1, 1:784]),
  nrow=28,
  ncol=28
)


image(
    t(img1[28:1, ]),
    col = gray.colors(256),
    axes = FALSE,
    useRaster = TRUE,
    main = paste(
      "Actual:", mnist_df$digit[1]
    )
  )


```

You have to reverse the order of the rows because it is stored with the first row representing the top of the image but the `image` function treats the first row as the bottom.  

Our first task will be to build a simple neural network which can predict the digits from the pixels using `nnet`. We'll select a sample of just 1000 images for our training set and 500 for test just to speed things up. Please do feel free to try a larger version if you're bored

```{r}
set.seed(1123)
n=nrow(mnist_df)
N=1000
indices = sample(n,N+500)

train = mnist_df[indices[1:N], ]
test = mnist_df[indices[(N+1):(N+500)], ]
```


```{r}
library(nnet)
digit_nnet=nnet(digit~.,
                data=train,
                size=10,
                MaxNWts=8000,
                trace=FALSE)
```

We didn't use the `MaxNWts` input before but need it here because the default is to restrict the network to 1000 weights. With 784 inputs, 10 hidden units, and 10 possible outputs (0-9), we have 
$$
(784+1)\times 10 = 7850
$$
weights going from the inputs to the hidden layer (the "+1" for the bias) and 
$$
(10+1)\times10 = 110
$$
going from hidden to output; see the theory supplement for further details about weights. 

Now let's look at the predictions on the test set

```{r}
yhat=predict(digit_nnet,newdata=test,type="class")
sum(test$digit==yhat)/500
```

Considering how shitty the handwriting is on some of these, that's not bad. For instance, let's look at a few of the incorrect ones.

```{r}
# Find incorrectly classified observations
incorrect = which(yhat != test$digit)

# Select the first 12
incorrect_12 = incorrect[1:12]

# Set up plotting grid
par(mfrow = c(3, 4), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))

for (i in incorrect_12) {

  img = matrix(
    as.numeric(test[i, 1:784]),
    nrow = 28,
    ncol = 28
  )

  image(
    t(img[28:1, ]),
    col = gray.colors(256),
    axes = FALSE,
    useRaster = TRUE,
    main = paste(
      "Actual:", test$digit[i],
      "\nPredicted:", yhat[i]
    )
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Some of those ARE pretty bad but I feel like we could do better. One thing we can do is increase the size of our training data. I tried the running the same code above with 10,000 training examples and did get closer to 90% accuracy. But for additional power, we need to be able to fine tune our network architecture and that requires introducing the `torch` package.

## Light `em up

Hopefully by this point you have caved and decided to watch at least the a few videos of 3blue1brown's series and/or read the theoretical supplement because its about to get real hot if not. In particularly, you'll need to have at least a vague notion of the following terms to understand what's going on here:

* activation funtions
* cost functions
* back-propagation

The `torch` package is a much more comprehensive and modern toolbox for fitting neural networks to data. It is capable of fitting multilayer feedforward networks with as many hidden units as we like. It starts with a definition of a model. Here we will use two hidden layers, each with 128 hidden units^[AI says computers like it when you choose hidden units in powers of 2. You are speaking their love language.] and ReLu activation functions^[`nnet` uses sigmoid but ReLu is faster and better.]


```{r}
library(torch)
digit_nn=nn_sequential(
  # Input to first hidden
  nn_linear(784,128),
  nn_relu(),
  
  # First to second hidden
  nn_linear(128,64),
  nn_relu(),
  
  #Second hidden to output
  nn_linear(64,10)
)

```

Now the annoying part. We have to redefine all of our training and testing sets as "tensors^[In math, tensors are multilinear maps. In computer/data science, they are just multidimensional array. Think matrices except you can have more than two indices.].".

```{r}
# Convert pixel values to tensors
x_train = torch_tensor(
  as.matrix(train[, 1:784]),
  dtype = torch_float()
)

x_test = torch_tensor(
  as.matrix(test[, 1:784]),
  dtype = torch_float()
)

# Convert digit labels to integers 1 through 10
y_train = torch_tensor(
  as.integer(as.character(train$digit)) + 1,
  dtype = torch_long()
)

y_test = torch_tensor(
  as.integer(as.character(test$digit)) + 1,
  dtype = torch_long()
)
```

Hopefully that is pretty self-explanatory except maybe the "+1" stuff at the end. That is just because `torch` expects class labels starting at 1 instead of 0. 

Now we need a couple additional definitions. First, the type of loss/cost function we will be minimizing. Using squared errors doesn't work so well for classification problems so here we use cross entropy^[More on this in the supplement. Maybe. It hasn't been fully written yet.]. Second, the optimizer part tells `torch` what algorithm to use for minimizing the loss via backpropagation. In this case, we set this equal to "Adam's" algorithm^[Hopefully not as depressing as Adam's Song. Ok fine, Adam isn't a person here. Its an acronym for ADAptive Moment estimation]. In contrast, `nnet` uses a different optimizer called BFGS^[Acronym for Bad Fucking GeniuS. or the initials of the researchers who came up with it, I'll let you decide.]. 

```{r}
model = digit_nn

loss_fn = nn_cross_entropy_loss()

optimizer = optim_adam(
  model$parameters,
  lr = 0.001
)
```




Now we train the model. You might be wondering what's up with the whole epoch and batch-size thing^[Which should be the name of a sitcom about two outcast aliens from different civilizations who become friends and triumph over the evil ruling Syndicate against all odds.]. Mini-batch gradient descent is a training method in which we split the data into smaller chunks called batches. After randomizing the initial weights, we use the first batch to calculate the loss function and perform a step of gradient descent to update the weights. We use the update weights to calculate the loss and perform another gradient descent step using the second batch and so on until we have gone through the entire training set. 

Smaller batch sizes make things more computationally manageable for larger dataset and let us update weights more frequently. This additional variability in gradient estimates can lead to a more thorough exploration of parameter spaces, potentially improving generalitzation. 

After the algorithm uses all batches, an epoch ends Then we reshuffle the observations into batches all over again and start the second epoch using the weights from the end of the previous epoch as its starting values. 

The code below performs these training steps. You can basically copy and paste it for reuse in other examples provided you change the model and training/testing data appropriately.

```{r}
epochs = 30
batch_size = 64

for (epoch in 1:epochs) {
  
  # Reset loss for current epoch
  total_loss = 0
  
  # Shuffle observations for current epoch
  order = sample.int(nrow(train))
  
  for (i in seq(1, length(order), by = batch_size)) {
    
    idx = order[i:min(i + batch_size - 1, length(order))]
    
    # Clears gradients from previous batch
    optimizer$zero_grad()
    
    # Calculate model output for current batch
    output = model(x_train[idx, ]) 

    # Calculate loss function for current model    
    loss = loss_fn(output, y_train[idx]) 
    
    # Calculate gradient of loss via backpropagation
    loss$backward()
    
    # Update weights
    optimizer$step()
    
    # Update loss function 
    total_loss = total_loss + loss$item()
  }
  
  # Print shit to see convergence
  cat(
    "Epoch:", epoch,
    "Average loss:", round(total_loss / ceiling(length(order) / batch_size), 4),
    "\n"
  )
}
```


The next code chunk does the fun part: prediction. 
```{r}
# Calculate predictions - basically like using predict with classes
test_output = model(x_test)
predictions = test_output$argmax(dim = 2)

# Convert predictions from 1-10 back to 0-9.
predicted_digits = as.integer(as_array(predictions)) - 1
actual_digits = as.integer(as.character(test$digit))

# Calculate test accuracy 
mean(predicted_digits == actual_digits)

```

We can see we did start to get some improvements with our sample of size 1000. With a larger sample size of 10000, I was able to get 95-96% accuracy and it was much faster than using `nnet` too. Consider that shit torched.

One additional comment if you plan to use torch for more complicate nnet fitting. Some models behave differently in training vs evaluation mode so it is best practice to insert the command `model$train()` before training a model and `model$eval()` before calculating predictions. I left them off here for simplicity and because they don't make a difference for the multilayer feedforward network we're fitting but you'll probably see them if you look up code online so now you know.  

## Autoencoders and Image Compression

Another application of neural networks is in image compression. The goal of this application is to take an image and encode it in a compressed format along with instructions on how to decode the compressed image back into its original format. 

To train a neural network for this type of task, we feed the images as both input and output. We funnel the input through a series of hidden layers. The middle one acts as a "bottleneck" with a smal number of units (32 in the example below). The encoder part compresses the original 784 pixels into a representation of only 32 numbers (from the bottleneck) and the decoder part uses these 32 numbers to reconstruct the original image. A neural network built through this procedure is called an _autoencoder_.  

To define an autoencoder for the digit data, we'll start by defining our model 


```{r}
autoencoder=nn_sequential(
  # First encoder layer
  nn_linear(784,128),
  nn_relu(),
  
  # Bottleneck
  nn_linear(128,32),
  nn_relu(),
  
  # First Decoder layer
  nn_linear(32,128),
  nn_relu(),
  
  # Output
  nn_linear(128,784),
  nn_sigmoid()
)

```


This time we will use the mean squared loss since the output (grayscale^[You'll notice I used both American and British spellings of gray/grey in these notes. Just trying to be unbiased. Except when it comes to writing words like center or meter. We all know spelling them centre or metre is just wrong. And I'm not adding an extra "u" in color. But daemon? That's cool. I just dont' really have a good reason to throw the word demon into my notes that often.] value) is numeric:

```{r}
model = autoencoder

loss_fn = nn_mse_loss()

optimizer = optim_adam(
  model$parameters,
  lr = 0.001
)

```

Now let's redefine our training and testing sets because we are going to need more than 1000 observations to train all the weights. 

```{r}
n=nrow(mnist_df)
N=10000
indices = sample(n,N+500)

train = mnist_df[indices[1:N], ]
test = mnist_df[indices[(N+1):(N+500)], ]

x_train = torch_tensor(
  as.matrix(train[, 1:784]),
  dtype = torch_float()
)

x_test = torch_tensor(
  as.matrix(test[, 1:784]),
  dtype = torch_float()
)
```

Then we'll do the training step. The only difference from our previous code is that we use `x_train` when calculating the loss instead of a separate `y_train` for digits. In other words, we are training the autoencoder to recognize the inputs themselves. 

```{r}
model$train()
epochs = 30
batch_size = 64

epoch_loss = numeric(epochs)

for (epoch in 1:epochs) {
  
  
  total_loss = 0
  
  order = sample.int(nrow(train))

  for (i in seq(1, length(order), by = batch_size)) {

    idx = order[i:min(i + batch_size - 1, length(order))]

    optimizer$zero_grad()

    output = model(x_train[idx, ])

    loss = loss_fn(output, x_train[idx, ])

    loss$backward()
    optimizer$step()

    total_loss = total_loss + loss$item()
  }

  epoch_loss[epoch] = total_loss / ceiling(length(order) / batch_size)

  cat(
    "Epoch:", epoch,
    "Average loss:", round(epoch_loss[epoch], 5),
    "\n"
  )
}
```

Now we'll calculate the predictions on the test set. 

```{r}
model$eval()

reconstructed = model(x_test)

reconstructed = as_array(reconstructed)

```


And then compare the first four

```{r}

par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))

for (i in 1:4) {

  original = matrix(
    as.numeric(x_test[i, ]),
    nrow = 28,
    ncol = 28
  )

  predicted = matrix(
    reconstructed[i, ],
    nrow = 28,
    ncol = 28
  )

  image(
    t(original[28:1, ]),
    col = gray.colors(256),
    axes = FALSE,
    useRaster = TRUE,
    main = "Original"
  )

  image(
    t(predicted[28:1, ]),
    col = gray.colors(256),
    axes = FALSE,
    useRaster = TRUE,
    main = "Reconstructed"
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
They're a little blurry but recognizable. You can choose to explore better options in the practice problems below.
